quotes.text: Nobody joins for the desks. They join because the third time they walk in, somebody says their name.
quotes.context: Responding to a question about why members renew.

quotes.text: We spend six weeks onboarding someone's key fob and zero minutes onboarding the person.
The ground floor should belong to the street. If a stranger can't wander in and feel something, the building is just storage.
quotes.context: During the debate about opening the café to non-members.

quotes.text: Half of us pay precisely because it's quiet. You open those doors and you've sold the one thing I can't get anywhere else.
quotes.context: Pushing back on the open-ground-floor proposal.

quotes.text: We're subsidising the people who need it least. The freelancers pay full whack and the funded organisations get mates' rates.
Grants are rent with extra homework. Every pound comes with a report attached, and the reports are eating the programme manager.
The café loses money making the place worth paying for. That's not a loss, that's marketing we happen to serve in cups.
The best event we ran was an accident — two members arguing about compost by the noticeboard and forty people stayed two hours.
quotes.context: On what the programme should learn from.

quotes.text: Members don't want another panel. They want the keys, the projector, and permission.
Consensus is how we avoid deciding. We call it inclusion, but really it's insurance against being blamed.
The board knows the accounts and the members know the building. The whole problem is those two groups meet twice a year.
quotes.context: On the gap between board and membership.

quotes.text: The Tuesday crowd and the Thursday crowd have never met. We're running two communities on one postcode.
